stem: You are examining the pharmacokinetics of calcium channel antagonists and are struck by the much lower dose of verapamil used in the treatment of atrial fibrillation when delivered intravenously versus orally (5 mg IV typically versus 120 mg or more given in divided doses orally). Which of the following pharmacokinetic factors best accounts for the difference in dosing?
explanation:
Bioavailability
The bioavailability of verapamil is severely impacted by first pass metabolism. Despite around 90% absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, extensive hepatic metabolism means that bioavailability is only 20%. Delivering the dose intravenously removes the impact of first pass metabolism. Peak plasma concentration is achieved approximately 1–2 h after oral administration.

Absorption
Absorption is incorrect. Verapamil is subject to good gastrointestinal absorption.

Half-life
Half-life is incorrect. Verapamil half-life is around 2–5 h, which determines the duration of drug effect rather than the dose.

Protein binding
Protein binding is incorrect. Verapamil is around 90% protein bound in the circulation, irrespective of whether administered orally or intravenously.

Renal clearance
Renal clearance is incorrect. Renal clearance has some impact on the duration of verapamil action, but would be the same if administered orally or intravenously.

stem: Which of the following is the best course of action?
options: IV normal saline and omit lithium for a short period
Stop indapamide, encourage oral fluids and omit lithium for a short period
explanation:
Stop indapamide, encourage oral fluids and omit lithium for a short period
Thiazide diuretics can precipitate lithium toxicity, and although the lithium level of 1.5 may not be immediately life threatening, it is high enough to be the cause of moderate to severe symptoms. The most appropriate course of action would be to stop the indapamide and omit the lithium for a short period to allow concentrations to fall, and then lithium could be restarted with therapeutic monitoring.

Activated charcoal
Activated charcoal is incorrect. Activated charcoal does not adsorb lithium and would not be expected to alter absorption.

Forced alkaline diuresis
Forced alkaline diuresis is incorrect. Forced alkaline diuresis is ineffective and potentially hazardous.

Haemodialysis
Haemodialysis is incorrect. Haemodialysis is highly effective in removing circulating lithium, but is normally reserved for patients with severe toxicity or when severe toxicity is likely based upon high circulating concentrations.

stem: You are evaluating a single dose study for a new twice-a-day medication for the treatment of hyperglycaemia. The peak concentration of the drug is reached 1 h after administration, and is found to be 800 μmol/l. The halflife is 3 h. What is the plasma concentration 15 h post-peak?
explanation:
25 μmol/l
25 μmol/l 15 h is equal to five half-lives, and for each half-life the concentration of the drug reduces by 50%. Therefore, over five half-lives it reduces to 1/32 of the original peak concentration, which in this case is 25 μmol/l. With respect to dosing, a longer half-life is optimal, as this allows for once-a-day dosing. Most agents which are dosed once per day have a half-life of >6–8 h.

50 μmol/l
50 μmol/l is incorrect. This is the concentration after four half-lives, namely 12 h.

100 μmol/l
100 μmol/l is incorrect. This is the concentration after three half-lives, namely 9 h.

200 μmol/l
200 μmol/l is incorrect. This is the concentration after two half-lives, namely 6 h.

400 μmol/l
400 μmol/l is incorrect. This is the concentration after one half-life, namely 3 h.

stem: A 57-year-old man who is treated with multiple therapies for hypertension, cardiovascular disease and Type 2 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. Over the past few months he has been suffering from increasingly severe mouth ulcers which are unresponsive to mouth washes and topical salicylate. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the ulceration?
explanation:
Nicorandil
Gastrointestinal ulceration, skin and mucosal ulceration have all been reported with nicorandil. These are refractory to antibiotics and corticosteroid treatment. If ulceration develops, nicorandil should be discontinued and this normally allows ulceration to resolve. Gastrointestinal perforation may occur when nicorandil and corticosteroids are combined, and the two should only be used cautiously.

Indapamide
Indapamide is incorrect. Indapamide may cause metabolic disturbance, including hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia.

Nifedipine
Nifedipine is incorrect. Nifedipine is associated with gingival hypertrophy rather than gastrointestinal tract ulceration.

Ramipril
Ramipril is incorrect. Ramipril is associated with cough, hyperkalaemia and kidney disease.

Valsartan
Valsartan is incorrect. Valsartan may cause hyperkalaemia and kidney disease, especially in patients with renovascular disease.

stem: You plan to intensify his glucose control. Which of the following would be an appropriate target with respect to his HbA1c?
explanation:
53 mmol/mol (7.0%)
NICE guidelines state that patients who are taking a medication associated with hypoglycaemia, as seen here, should have a target of 53mmol/mol (7.0%). More aggressive targets put the patient at the risk of hypoglycaemic episodes. Previous clinical studies, the ACCORD and VADT trials, attempted to achieve a very tight HbA1c target of 42 mmol/mol (6%) in an attempt to reduce the risk of vascular complications of diabetes, but found that intensive glucose control was associated with a small increase in sudden cardiovascular death. The mechanism may have been increased sympathetic drive or electrolyte imbalance at the time of hypoglycaemia episodes, which could have caused arrhythmia.

40 mmol/mol (5.8%)
40 mmol/mol (5.8%) is incorrect. This target is too low for any patient with type 2 diabetes, and would be associated with a hazard of hypoglycaemia.

48 mmol/mol (6.5%)
48 mmol/mol (6.5%) is incorrect. This is the target for patients who are managed by diet or medications, such as metformin, that are not associated with hypoglycaemia. Aiming for this target in this patient may runs the risk of such episodes.

65 mmol/mol (8.1%)
65 mmol/mol (8.1%) is incorrect. This may be an appropriate target for some patients that are prone to hypoglycaemia but is insufficient for reducing the complications of diabetes. Whilst NICE guidelines do state that HbA1c levels can be relaxed on a ‘case-by-case’ basis for patients who are older or frail we have no evidence of frailty in them.

74 mmol/mol (8.9%)
74 mmol/mol (8.9%) is incorrect. This is an insufficient target for reducing the complications of diabetes.

stem: You are asked to review the primaquine prescription for a 28-year-old student who has been admitted to the acute medical ward for treatment of Plasmodium vivax malaria. What is the main pharmacological mechanism of action of primaquine in the management of malaria?
options: Removal of gametocytes from the blood
Removal of hypnozoites from the liver
Removal of merozoites from the blood
Removal of oocytes from the blood
Removal of sporozoites from the blood
explanation:
Removal of hypnozoites from the liver
Primaquine is an 8-aminoquinolone used in the treatment of Plasmodium vivax or Plasmodium ovale malaria. Once the parasite has been eliminated from the bloodstream, the remaining hypnozoites must be removed from the liver and this is achieved with a 14-day course of primaquine. Without addition of primaquine, there is a very high risk of relapse. It should not be given to patients with severe G6PD deficiency because of a high risk of haemolysis; WHO guidelines indicate that primaquine may be considered where G6PD deficiency is mild to moderate. Primaquine is usually administered in combination with chloroquine, a higher dose (30 mg/day) is given for vivax malaria compared with ovale (15 mg/day).

Removal of gametocytes from the blood
Removal of gametocytes from the blood is incorrect. Primaquine is used primarily to eradicate liver hypnozoites, rather than gametocytes from the blood.

Removal of merozoites from the blood
Removal of merozoites from the blood is incorrect. Primaquine is used primarily to eradicate liver hypnozoites, rather than merozoites from the blood.

Removal of oocytes from the blood
Removal of oocytes from the blood is incorrect. Primaquine is used primarily to eradicate liver hypnozoites, rather than oocytes from the blood.

Removal of sporozoites from the blood
Removal of sporozoites from the blood is incorrect. Primaquine is used primarily to eradicate liver hypnozoites, rather than sporozoites from the blood.

stem: A patient with learning disability and epilepsy requires occasional emergency treatment for generalised tonic– clonic seizures. What most accounts for the rapid onset of action of diazepam?
explanation:
Rapid distribution
Diazepam is highly lipid soluble and highly protein bound, The volume of distribution is 0.8 to 1.0 L/kg. Peak concentrations of diazepam within the brain are reached within 5 min after intravenous administration.

Extended half-life when given IV
Diazepam is eliminated slowly over 1–2 days after administration, but this is unrelated to its onset of action.

Lack of first pass metabolism
Diazepam is extensively metabolised by the liver to a number of active metabolites, hence liver metabolism does not significantly impact on its therapeutic effect.

Protein binding
Diazepam is heavily protein bound, and observes a biphasic fall in plasma concentrations; there is initial rapid distribution to tissues related to its protein binding and lipid solubility, followed by slow and persisting elimination over 1–2 days. Therefore, the protein binding will have little effect.

Water solubility
Diazepam has limited water solubility, and the parenteral formulation is presented in a soya emulsion.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms and laboratory findings?
explanation:
Trimethoprim-related pancytopaenia
Trimethoprim is a recognised cause of pancytopaenia, isolated leucopaenia, megaloblastic anaemia, thrombocytopaenia and agranulocyctosis. Trimethoprim is a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor, which may lead to a clinically significant reduction in folic acid incorporation in the bone marrow.

Allopurinol-related pancytopaenia
Allopurinol-related pancytopaenia is incorrect. Allopurinol may cause immunosuppression, and bone marrow failure may occur in patients taking azathioprine in addition because the interaction causes toxic levels of 6mercaptopurine.

ITP
ITP is incorrect. ITP would not explain the anaemia and low white count.

Ramipril-related pancytopaenia
Ramipril-related pancytopaenia is incorrect. The occurrence of pancytopaenia related to ACE inhibitors is very rare.

TTP
TTP in incorrect. TTP would be unexpected in the absence of a preceding diarrhoeal illness or other history suggestive of Escherichia coli exposure.

stem: In respect of the pharmacokinetics of digoxin, which characteristic drives the requirement for a loading dose?
explanation:
Volume of distribution
Digoxin has a large volume of distribution and readily penetrates tissues, including heart, brain, erythrocytes and skeletal muscles, and crosses the blood–brain barrier. The concentration of digoxin in the myocardium is considerably higher than in plasma. The volume of distribution is decreased in patients with renal impairment and hypothyroidism and it is increased in patients with hyperthyroidism.

Bioavailability
Bioavailability is incorrect. The oral bioavailability of digoxin is around 70%, which makes it well suited to oral administration.

First pass metabolism
First pass metabolism is incorrect. Digoxin is predominantly subject to renal elimination, and first pass metabolism is not clinically relevant.

Half-life
Half-life is incorrect. Half-life determines the duration of action of digoxin, rather than the time to achieve therapeutic drug concentrations. The half-life is around 40 h, and prolonged significantly in patients with renal impairment so that the dosing interval should be increased, or dose reduced.

Protein binding
Protein binding is incorrect. Around 20 to 30% of digoxin dose is bound to plasma proteins, although it is not protein binding which determines the necessity for a loading dose.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is morbidly obese. She has a history of multiple DVTs for which she is on long-term warfarin, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, epilepsy and tuberculosis. Her GP has referred her to the Emergency Department because of an increase in her INR to 5.0. The patient tells you that her medications have recently been altered. On examination, her BP is 135/75 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. Her BMI is 32. There are no signs of active bleeding. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of the increase in INR?
explanation:
Erythromycin
Erythromycin is a CYP 3A4 inhibitor; as such it potentiates the action of warfarin, simvastatin and other drugs metabolised by this cytochrome. The interaction between erythromycin and warfarin causes an increased INR and bleeding risk. Other agents capable of inhibiting warfarin metabolism include allopurinol, disulfiram, ketoconazole, omeprazole, cimetidine, glibenclamide, metronidazole and amiodarone.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is incorrect. Carbamazapine is a powerful enzyme inducer, which enhances the extent of warfarin metabolism so that INR falls.

Glimepiride
Glimepiride is incorrect. Glimepiride is a highly protein-bound sulfonylurea. Displacement from protein-binding sites may slightly increase warfarin effects and raise INR; however, the effect would be significantly less than that observed from the interaction with erythromycin.

Phenytoin
Phenytoin is incorrect. Phenytoin is a potent enzyme inducer that increases the rate and extent of warfarin metabolism so that INR falls.

Rifampicin
Rifampicin is incorrect. Rifampicin suppresses the anticoagulant activity of warfarin, which can lead to a need for increased doses of warfarin to achieve and maintain a therapeutic INR; furthermore frequent INR monitoring is needed even after discontinuing rifampicin. This is due to the induction of microsomal enzymes which leads to the catabolism of warfarin resulting in suppression of warfarin activity. Withdrawal of rifampicin decreases the warfarin requirement by 50%.

stem: Activity of which enzyme can be assayed to determine the risk of leukopaenia when starting azathioprine therapy?
explanation:
Thiopurine methyltransferase
TPMT is responsible for a key step in the metabolism of azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine (the active metabolite of azathioprine). Genetically determined deficiency of TPMT leads to accumulation of 6mercaptopurine, resulting in neutropaenia. Approximately 10% of patients have a genetic polymorphism that causes deficient TPMT activity.

Glucuronyl transferase
Glucuronyl transferase is incorrect. Glucuronyl transferase deficiency is responsible for Gilbert’s syndrome, characterised by high fasting bilirubin concentrations.

Hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase
Hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase is incorrect. Hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase is a step in purine nucleotide generation.

N-acetyl transferase
N-acetyl transferase is incorrect. N-acetyl transferase is involved in acetylation of a number of different drugs, normally a step in drug inactivation but occasionally acetylation may cause formation of an active drug from a prodrug.

Xanthine oxidase
Xanthine oxidase is incorrect. Xanthine oxidase is the rate limiting step in purine metabolism to urate; inhibition by drugs including allopurinol or febuxostat reduces urate formation and serum concentrations fall by 25–30%.

stem: A 45-year-old man plans a trip to Africa with his family. He has a history of G6PD deficiency. Which of the following anti-malarials would be most hazardous in this patient and should be avoided?
explanation:
Primaquine
Patients with G6PD deficiency are prone to red cell oxidative stress, and a number of agents are known to increase the risk of red cell oxidative stress and lead to a haemolytic crisis. Out of the options given, it is primaquine that is most associated with risk of haemolysis, which may occur even in the absence of G6PD deficiency. Quinolones and sulfonamides confer a high risk of haemolysis and should be avoided in patients with G6PD deficiency.

Chloroquine
Chloroquine is incorrect. Chloroquine and quinine also carry some risk of haemolysis, although in most cases the benefit of using them is thought to outweigh potential risks. Haemolysis is less likely to occur than with primaquine.

Doxycycline
Doxycycline is incorrect. Doxycycline is unlikely to cause haemolysis.

Mefloquine
Mefloquine is incorrect. Mefloquine is less likely to cause haemolysis than primaquine, chloroquine, or quinine.

Proguanil
Proguanil is incorrect. Proguanil is less likely to cause haemolysis than primaquine.

stem: A 36-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She is in her second pregnancy. There is a history of preeclampsia in her first pregnancy by a different partner. She has mild hypertension but no other past medical history of note. On examination her BP is 155/90 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and regular. Her BMI is 34. Which of the following is most effective in reducing future risk of pre-eclampsia?
explanation:
Aspirin 75 mg daily
A number of trials of low-dose aspirin in prevention of pre-eclampsia in high-risk individuals have been reported. A meta-analysis of over 11 000 women suggests that a low dose commenced prior to week 16 confers a 50% relative risk reduction in the incidence of pre-eclampsia. No benefit was obtained when aspirin was started after week 16.

Aspirin 300 mg daily
Aspirin 300 mg daily is incorrect. Aspirin doses higher than 75 mg are not expected to confer any additional benefit over lower doses but are associated with an increased bleeding risk.

Daily low-molecular-weight heparin
Daily low-molecular-weight heparin is incorrect. Daily low-molecular-weight heparin is used in patients who are anti-phospholipid antibody positive with a history of recurrent miscarriage.

Nifedipine MR 60 mg daily
Nifedipine MR 60 mg daily is incorrect. Nifedipine may be used as a treatment for hypertension in pregnancy, or labetalol.

Salt restriction
Salt restriction is incorrect. Based upon the patient’s weight and blood pressure, salt and calorie restriction would be advised, but these alone would be less effective than aspirin therapy. Prescribing Safely (Breastfeeding and Pregnancy).

stem: A 28-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with status epilepticus and is treated with IV lorazepam. Which of the following most correctly represents the pharmacological mechanism of action of lorazepam?
explanation:
GABA (gamma-Aminobutyric acid) agonist
GABA-A receptors have multiple binding sites for a range of compounds including benzodiazepines and barbiturates. Benzodiazepines including lorazepam are used as an acute treatment for epilepsy because of rapid transfer across the blood–brain barrier and prompt onset of action. The development of tolerance means that both benzodiazepines and barbiturates are not normally used as long-term sole therapies in the treatment of epilepsy.

GABA reuptake inhibitor
GABA reuptake inhibitor is incorrect. Tiagabine is an example of a GABA reuptake inhibitor.

GABA transaminase inhibitor
GABA transaminase inhibitor is incorrect. Vigabatrin is thought to inhibit GABA transaminase, therefore enhancing GABA concentrations and lowering glutamate concentrations within the central nervous system. GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter wherease glutamate is a stimulatory neurotransmitter.

Glutamate blocker
Glutamate blocker is incorrect. Glutamate inhibitors include topiramate.

Neuronal potassium channel activator
Neuronal potassium channel activator is incorrect. The most well-known neural potassium channel activator is retigabine.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with multiple medical problems is admitted to the Emergency Department with progressive confusion over the past six weeks. She has a history of depression, diabetes and hypertension. On examination her BP is 135/72 mmHg, pulse is 70 bpm and regular. Her BMI is 25. Venous blood gas sampling reveals a sodium level of 118 mmol/l. Which of the following medications is most likely to have caused hyponatraemia in this patient?
explanation:
Bendroflumethiazide
In this case the patient probably has hypontraemia as a result of Bendroflumethiazide causing increased sodium loss. The drugs most commonly implicated in SIADH as a cause of hyponatraemia include vinca alkaloids, cyclophosphamide, carbamazepine, phenothiazines, tricyclic antidepressants, morphine and nicotine.

Atorvastatin
Atorvastatin is incorrect. Statin therapy is not known to cause hyponatraemia.

Fluoxetine
Fluoxetine is incorrect. Fluoxetine and other SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) antidepressants may cause hyponatraemia, but less commonly and less pronounced than thiazides, hence bendroflumethiazide is the preferred option chosen here.

Gliclazide
Gliclazide is incorrect. Gliclazide may rarely cause hyponatraemia.

Ramipril
Ramipril is incorrect. ACE inhibitors do not characteristically cause hyponatraemia; hyperkalaemia is a wellrecognised adverse effect.

stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department with symptoms of a urinary tract infection with suprapubic pain. A urine specimen is positive for blood, protein and nitrites. She has had a previous anaphylactic reaction to benzylpenicillin. She is breastfeeding a 5-month-old baby and wants to continue feeding the infant if possible. Which of the following antibiotics is the most appropriate to give her?
explanation:
Trimethoprim
Trimethoprim is normally effective against a range of organisms capable of causing lower urinary tract infections. It may interfere with folate metabolism, which carries a risk of neural tube defects in preganancy; however, a short treatment course, e.g. 5 days, would not be expected to pose any significant hazard.

Amoxicillin
Amoxicillin is incorrect. The prior history of penicillin allergy would make this treatment potentially hazardous.

Cephalexin
Cephalexin is incorrect. The evidence for cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins has changed in recent years. Previously, a 20% cross-allergy had been quoted but this is now thought to stem largely from contamination of cephalosporin products with trace amounts of penicillin in the manufacturing process. The most recent quoted figures are <1% in patients with penicillin allergy but no confirmatory skin testing, and ~2% in those with confirmed positive penicillin skin testing. With all this in mind, in current practice, for a severe allergic response like anaphylaxis, cephalosporins are still an absolute contra-indication and hence is not an appropriate choice for this patient.

Ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin is incorrect. Quinolones are contra-indicated in children due to the risk of tendon rupture, and if the mother continues to breast feed there is a risk to the child.

Doxycycline
Doxycycline is incorrect. Tetracyclines are contraindicated in children due to uptake into developing bones and teeth causing dental discoloration.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is reviewed in the Multi-Disciplinary Breast Clinic after undergoing right lumpectomy for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer. She has a past history of hypertension for which she takes ramipril and indapamide, and depression for which she has been taking fluoxetine but nil else of note. Long-term tamoxifen is recommended. Which of the following is the most important treatment consideration with respect to tamoxifen?
options: Indapamide should be changed to an alternative
Risk of venous thromboembolism will be increased two–three-fold
Risk of ovarian cancer is increased
explanation:
Fluoxetine
Drugs that are metabolised via the CYP2D6 route have significant interaction potential with respect to tamoxifen. CYP2D6 inhibitors prevent formation of endoxifen, an important active metabolite of tamoxifen and, therefore, may significantly reduce drug efficacy. Potent CYP2D6 inhibitors include paroxetine, fluoxetine, quinidine and bupropion.

Indapamide should be changed to an alternative
Indapamide should be changed to an alternative is incorrect. There is no significant interaction between indapamide and tamoxifen.

Risk of venous thromboembolism will be increased two–three-fold
Tamoxifen does increase the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE), which is an important consideration. However, in the context of this patient, the immediate impact of the interaction between fluoxetine and tamoxifen is more critical because it directly affects the efficacy of tamoxifen in treating breast cancer. While the risk of VTE is significant, it is a known risk that is generally managed and monitored in patients receiving tamoxifen. The interaction with fluoxetine, on the other hand, requires immediate attention to ensure the patient receives the full benefit of the tamoxifen therapy.

Triglycerides may increase
Triglycerides may increase is incorrect. Tamoxifen does cause increased triglyceride concentrations, but this is a much less important consideration overall than the immediate impact of the fluoxetine–tamoxifen drug interaction.

Risk of ovarian cancer is increased
Risk of ovarian cancer is increased is incorrect. There is controversy regarding the possibility that tamoxifen might increase ovarian cancer risk in pre-menopausal women, although there are no convincing data. Liver Enzyme Inhibition You are auditing the prescription of hormone replacement therapy for patients within the trust catchment area.

stem: A 47-year-old public house owner is brought to the Emergency Department by his wife. He has had influenza for the past 48 hrs and has been confined to his bed. Although his cold symptoms have improved, he is becoming agitated, says there are monkeys clustered around the room, and he has insects crawling over his skin. He is known to drink 10 pints of beer and one-third of a bottle of whisky per day. On arrival in the Emergency Department he is extremely agitated and sweating profusely. His BP is 155/85 mmHg and pulse is 100/min and regular. He tries to fight you off as you examine him, but he says he will accept some tablets to help calm him down. A finger- prick glucose is 8.1 mmol/l. The patient remains agitated, which of the following is the most useful next medication?
explanation:
Chlordiazepoxide
A reducing dose of chlordiazepoxide given over 5–7 days is the usual treatment for unplanned alcohol withdrawal, with oral diazepam as an alternative. A typical regimen might be as follows: Day 1: 20 mg chlordiazepoxide four times daily. Day 2: 15 mg chlordiazepoxide four times daily. Day 3: 10 mg chlordiazepoxide four times daily. Day 4: 5 mg chlordiazepoxide four times daily. Day 5: 5 mg chlordiazepoxide twice daily.

Haloperidol
Haloperidol is incorrect. Haloperidol can be used as a rapid tranquiliser for agitated patients who are a harm to themselves or others but less restrictive, and more effective, options are available and should be tried first. Chlordiazepoxide, and in some regions diazepam, are used for alcohol withdrawal as a first line treatment.

Hypostop
Hypostop is incorrect. Hypostop is used as a treatment for acute hypoglycaemia but would not address the risk of seizures associated with acute alcohol withdrawal. Although glucose should be monitored, treatment of hypoglycaemia is not essential at this stage given a finger-prick glucose of 8.1 mmol/l.

Risperidone
Risperidone is incorrect. Risperidone is an atypical anti-psychotic and it is not routinely recommended in alcohol withdrawal.

Thiamine
Thiamine is incorrect. Consideration of thiamine replacement is essential. Immediate replacement may be given as two ampoules of Pabrinex® (each containing vitamins B1 125 mg, B2, B3, B6, vitamin C and anhydrous dextrose), followed by oral thiamine.

stem: You are auditing the prescription of hormone replacement therapy for patients within the trust catchment area. Which of the following is an indication for HRT?
options: First line for the treatment of atrophic vaginitis
First line for the treatment of osteoporosis
For night sweats more than 10 years after normal menopause
Premature ovarian failure until the age of 51
Within 1 year of cessation of periods in patients with normal menopause for night sweats
explanation:
Premature ovarian failure until the age of 51
Indications for HRT are significantly limited because of the increased risk of ischaemic cardiovascular disease, venous thromboembolism, breast cancer associated with its use. The benefit risk is, however, considered positive in patients with premature ovarian failure (<40 years), and in patients with osteoporosis who are not able to take other treatment options. Medication should not usually be started until more than a year after the cessation of periods. Some women still request HRT for debilitating peri-menopausal symptoms where it is important to consider the overall benefit versus risks of HRT treatment.

First line for the treatment of atrophic vaginitis
First line for the treatment of atrophic vaginitis is incorrect. Topical oestrogen preparations may be appropriate in this situation.

First line for the treatment of osteoporosis
First line for the treatment of osteoporosis is incorrect. Lifestyle measures and other bone health treatments are normally more effective and appropriate than HRT for osteoporosis alone.

For night sweats more than 10 years after normal menopause
For night sweats more than 10 years after normal menopause (Option C) is incorrect. It would be unusual for symptoms to persist for more than 10 years, and an alternative explanation should be sought.

Within 1 year of cessation of periods in patients with normal menopause for night sweats
Within 1 year of cessation of periods in patients with normal menopause for night sweats is incorrect. Treatment is normally deferred for 1 year after cessation of regular periods so that treatment may be avoided in patients where symptoms resolve spontaneously.

stem: You are asked to prescribe an antibiotic for a 72-year-old woman convalescing on the Elderly Care Ward after a left total hip replacement. She has developed symptoms of a lower urinary tract infection (UTI). Which of the following antimicrobials is likely to be safest and carries the lowest risk of Clostridioides difficile infection?
explanation:
Trimethoprim
Guidelines suggest that cephalosporins and broad-spectrum penicillins, such as co-amoxiclav, clindamycin and fluoroquinolones, are all associated with an increased risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. As such, the best option is trimethoprim, depending upon local organisms causing urinary tract infection and patterns of susceptibility and resistance. Guidelines also recommend minimising the length of antibiotic therapy as much as possible and avoiding widespread use of antibiotic use in the absence of clear evidence of infection.

Ceftriaxone
Ceftriaxone is incorrect. Ceftriaxone is available only for intravenous administration, which may be unneccesary in this patient according to severity of symptoms.

Cephalexin
Cephalexin is incorrect. Cephalosporins are associated with a particularly high rate of complication by C. difficile and other antibiotics.

Co-amoxiclav
Co-amoxiclav is incorrect. Co-amoxiclav may be indicated for severe infection so that the benefits of treatment would offset the comparatively minor risk of C. difficile infection.

Levofloxacin
Levofloxacin is incorrect. Levofloxacin and other quinolones are associated with an increased risk of C. difficile infection, non-specific gastroenteritis along with irreversible musculoskeletal and neurological adverse effects, especially in the elderly.

stem: A 35-year-old man being treated with multi-drug chemotherapy for tuberculosis is reviewed urgently because he has suffered a significant rise in his transaminases. You suspect this may be due to isoniazid toxicity. Which of the following is thought to increase the risk of isoniazid liver toxicity?
explanation:
Rapid acetylator status
Isoniazid is subject to metabolism by a number of specific pathways, including acetylation within the liver. Liver toxicity is related to a key metabolite of isoniazid, and the occurrence of this adverse effect is dependent upon acetylator status. Slow acetylator status causes high drug concentrations, which mediate peripheral neuropathy; in contrast, rapid acetylator status is associated with more extensive metabolite formation and increased hepatic toxicity due to its metabolite.

CYP-2D6 poor metaboliser status
Isoniazid is primarily metabolised by acetylation rather than by the CYP-2D6 pathway. Therefore, alterations in CYP-2D6 activity do not significantly impact isoniazid metabolism or toxicity. Slow acetylator status does confer a higher risk of peripheral neuropathy, but liver toxicity is linked to the production of acetylated metabolites.

OAT-1 inhibitor co-prescription
The OAT-1 renal transporter primarily affects the excretion of drugs via the kidneys. Isoniazid is extensively metabolised by the liver rather than being excreted unchanged by the kidneys. Consequently, inhibiting OAT-1 would have little effect on isoniazid's risk of causing liver toxicity.

P450 enzyme inducer co-prescription
While P450 enzymes play a role in the metabolism of many drugs, they contribute minimally to the metabolism of isoniazid. The major metabolic pathway for isoniazid is acetylation, controlled by the NAT2 enzyme. Therefore, inducing P450 enzymes would not significantly influence isoniazid hepatotoxicity.

P450 enzyme inhibitor co-prescription
Inhibiting P450 enzymes would have a negligible effect on the risk of isoniazid-related liver toxicity. The primary metabolic pathway for isoniazid involves acetylation via NAT2, rather than oxidative metabolism through P450 enzymes. Hepatitis associated with isoniazid is mostly caused by the acetylated metabolite, not by pathways involving P450 enzymes.

stem: Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of his presentation?
explanation:
Allopurinol
Nausea and vomiting are characteristic features of theophylline toxicity; metabolic acidosis and hypokalaemia are recognised complications. A number of co-prescribed medications cause increased theophylline drug concentrations, predominantly due to inhibition of hepatic metabolism, thereby increasing the risk of toxicity. Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor with additional non-specific inhibitory effects on hepatic P450 enzyme activity. Other drugs that provoke theophylline toxicity include: carbimazole cimetidine ciprofloxacin clarithromycin diltiazem disulfiram erythromycin fluconazole interferon isoniazid methotrexate thiabendazole verapamil.

Amoxicillin
Amoxicillin is incorrect. Amoxicillin is not expected to exert any direct effect on theophylline metabolism.

Metronidazole
Metronidazole is incorrect. Metronidazole inhibits acetaldehyde dehydrogenase but has only limited impact on theophylline metabolism.

Naproxen
Naproxen is incorrect. There are no reports of an interaction between theophylline and naproxen.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is incorrect. There is no clinically relevant interaction between prednisolone and theophylline, which are commonly co-administered in clinical practice.

stem: Urine is dipstick positive to blood What would you expect to find on urinalysis?
explanation:
Myoglobin
Clarithromycin is a potent inhibitor of CYP3A4 and causes a well-characterised interaction with drugs metabolised primarily by 3A4, including simvastatin and atorvastatin. Rhabdomyolysis is characterised by a large rise in CK, presence of myoglobinuria and renal impairment.

Casts
Casts is incorrect. Casts may be found across a number of renal conditions. Fatty casts/oval bodies are seen as a complication of nephrotic syndrome. Hyaline casts may be related to dehydration, exercise or diuretics. Red blood cell casts are seen across a range of glomerulonephritides. Renal tubular epithelial cell casts are seen in renal tubular necrosis, and in kidney transplant rejection. Waxy casts are seen in chronic kidney failure. White blood cell casts are seen in urinary tract infection.

Haemoglobin
Haemoglobin is incorrect. Haemoglobinuria may occur in the setting of acute glomerulonephritis.

Oval bodies
Oval bodies is incorrect. Oval casts may be seen in the setting of nephrotic syndrome.

Red blood cells
Red blood cells is incorrect. Red blood cells, haematuria may be due to trauma, infection, glomerular disease or malignancy affecting the urinary tract. Liver Enzyme Inhibition A 62-year-old man who suffered a TIA some 6 years ago comes to the clinic for review. He is taking a combination of aspirin and dipyridamole.

stem: A 62-year-old man who suffered a TIA some 6 years ago comes to the clinic for review. He is taking a combination of aspirin and dipyridamole. Which of the following best describes the pharmacological mechanism of action of dipyridamole?
explanation:
Phosphodiesterase inhibitor
Dipyridamole is a PDE inhibitor that leads to increased intracellular cyclic AMP; this in turn blocks the platelet response to ADP. Its combination with aspirin is more effective in stroke prevention than treatment with either drug alone. It has largely been replaced by clopidogrel based upon recommendations of NICE.

ADP receptor inhibitor
ADP receptor inhibitor is incorrect. Clopidogrel is an ADP receptor inhibitor.

COX-1 inhibitor
COX-1 inhibitor is incorrect. NSAIDs including aspirin are non-selective inhibitors of COX-1 and COX-2.

Factor Xa inhibitor
Factor Xa inhibitor is incorrect. Direct factor Xa inhibitors have recently become available for prophylaxis against VTE and embolism in AF. A useful advantage of these agents is that they do not require INR monitoring, although this may be a disadvantage where monitoring is considered desirable.

Thrombin inhibitor
Thrombin inhibitor is incorrect. Oral direct thrombin inhibitors have a role in the treatment of ACS, as an alternative to heparin when heparin-induced thrombocytopaenia (HIT) occurs.

stem: Which of the following is the cause of phenytoin toxicity in this situation?
explanation:
Decreased phenytoin protein binding
Phenytoin levels measure total drug, that is free and bound elements added together. Phenytoin and warfarin are highly protein bound (90% in the case of phenytoin), and uraemia is recognised to lead to an increased free component of each drug. In this case therefore the proportion of free versus bound phenytoin has increased, leading to symptoms of toxicity even though the total phenytoin level remains within the therapeutic range. Correction of uraemia should lead to a resolution of symptoms of phenytoin toxicity. Population groups that are predisposed to elevated free phenytoin levels include neonates, elderly persons, and individuals with uremia, hypoalbuminemia (due to pregnancy, nephrotic syndrome, malignancy, malnutrition), or hyperbilirubinemia. These patients may exhibit signs of toxicity when drug levels are within the therapeutic range.

Decreased phenytoin excretion
Decreased phenytoin excretion is incorrect. Phenytoin elimination remains unchanged.

Decreased phenytoin metabolism
Decreased phenytoin metabolism is incorrect. There is no impact on phenytoin metabolism, which is normally comparatively slow.

Increased phenytoin absorption
Increased phenytoin absorption is incorrect. Drug absorption may be impaired in kidney disease if there is significant oedema affecting the gastrointestinal tract. However, this would not give rise to increased phenytoin toxicity.

Increased phenytoin protein binding
Increased phenytoin protein binding is incorrect. Protein binding is decreased, not increased.

stem: A 19-year-old female presents to the Emergency Department by ambulance. According to her friends, she has been complaining of a headache and sore throat over the past few days. When they tried to wake her in the morning she had become drowsy and confused. Examination reveals pyrexia at 38.5 °C, her heart rate is 100 bpm and regular and her blood pressure is 85 mmHg. She has skin mottling with a maculopapular rash and areas of petechial haemorrhage. Her Glasgow coma score is 13 and she has obvious signs of meningism. You are unable to see her fundi. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
IV ceftriaxone
The clinical scenario is strongly suggestive of infection with Neisseria meningitidis, and guidelines recommend commencing IV ceftriaxone without delay. Vancomycin should be considered in addition if there has been recent foreign travel or exposure to recent multiple courses of antibiotics. Corticosteroids may minimise the extent of hearing loss and neurological sequelae, although they do not impact on overall mortality. Circulatory support, in the first instance with IV fluids, is also required.

IM penicillin
Pre-hospital administration of penicillin or cefotaxime is recommended, provided that administration does not delay transfer to hospital.

IV clarithromycin
Macrolide antibiotics are less active against N. meningitidis than penicillins or cephalosporins.

IV co-amoxiclav
Co-amoxiclav is not recommended in this situation due to unpredictable drug transfer across the blood–brain barrier.

IV penicillin
Penicillin penetration of the blood–brain barrier is inconsistent, and it may be less active against certain organisms including Haemophilus influenzae. Bacterial Meningitis A 43-year-old woman with a long-term history of manic depressive psychosis comes to the Emergency Department. She has nausea, diarrhoea and light-headedness, and feels weak and lethargic. Her lithium level is measured at 2.5 mmol/l. Recent history of note is that she has begun a course of metronidazole for a dental abscess.

stem: A 43-year-old woman with a long-term history of manic depressive psychosis comes to the Emergency Department. She has nausea, diarrhoea and light-headedness, and feels weak and lethargic. Her lithium level is measured at 2.5 mmol/l. Recent history of note is that she has begun a course of metronidazole for a dental abscess. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her lithium toxicity?
explanation:
Reduced renal clearance
Metronidazole is thought to reduce renal clearance of lithium and this is likely to have given rise to lithium toxicity in this patient. Other agents known to increase lithium concentrations are: non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, including cyclo-oxygenase (COX) 2 inhibitors, which cause increased sodium and lithium reabsorption at renal tubular level ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists thiazide diuretics, which cause increased renal lithium reabsorption corticosteroids, which may interfere with renal lithium elimination tetracyclines, due to renal interaction, although the exact mechanism unclear.

Decreased GI excretion
Decreased GI excretion is incorrect. Lithium is almost exclusively subject to renal excretion, and gastrointestinal elimination is irrelevant.

Decreased protein binding
Decreased protein binding is incorrect. Lithium is not protein bound, and is not subject to protein-binding interactions.

Increased absorption
Increased absorption is incorrect. Lithium is well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, and almost completely absorbed even after a very large dose.

Reduced metabolism
Reduced metabolism is incorrect. Lithium is not metabolised in the liver or elsewhere, so that 95% of a given dose is excreted in the urine.

stem: Which of the following co-prescribed antimicrobials is the most likely cause of the rise in creatinine?
explanation:
Fluconazole
All inhibitors of CYP3A4 and/or P-glycoprotein may lead to increased levels of ciclosporin, which characteristically causes hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury. Fluconazole, ketoconazole, itraconazole and voriconazole may more than double ciclosporin concentrations. Other medicines capable of provoking ciclosporin toxicity include: methylprednisolone (high dose), allopurinol, protease inhibitors and colchicine.

Azithromycin
Azithromycin is incorrect. Macrolide antibiotics may increase ciclosporin concentrations: erythromycin causes a four- to seven-fold increase in ciclosporin; clarithromycin may double ciclosporin concentrations; whereas azithromycin may cause only a minor increase in ciclosporin by around 20%. Azithromycin is less likely to provoke toxicity than is fluconazole, hence fluconazole is the preferred answer.

Cephalexin
Cephalexin is incorrect. Cephalexin is unlikely to significantly interact with ciclosporin.

Co-amoxiclav
Co-amoxiclav is incorrect. Co-amoxiclav is not expected to cause any significant interaction with ciclosporin.

Nifedipine
Nifedipine is incorrect. Nifedipine is unlikely to cause a significant pharmacokinetic interaction with ciclosporin, although both may cause gingival hyperplasia. In contrast, verapamil increases ciclosporin blood concentrations by two- to three-fold, and diltiazem by around 50%.

stem: A 46-year-old woman is in remission from chronic myelocytic leukaemia (CML) and is treated with imatinib. Which one of the following enzyme types is inhibited by imatinib?
explanation:
Tyrosine kinase
The fusion between the Abelson (Abl) tyrosine kinase gene at chromosome 9 and the break point cluster (Bcr) gene on chromosome 22 results in a chimeric oncogene (Bcr-Abl), the so-called Philidelphia chromosome. This is expressed in some types of CML. Imatinib inhibits Bcr-abl tyrosine kinase, which leads to selective inhibition of proliferation and apoptosis in cells that express Bcr-abl. Imatinib also inhibits platelet-derived growth factor tyrosine kinase, and it may be used in myeloproliferative or myelodysplastic disorders associated with plateletderived growth factor receptor expression, and for certain other other malignancies such as gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST).

DNA polymerase
DNA polymerase is incorrect. DNA polymerase forms DNA strands from individual deoxyribonucleotides.

DNA topoisomerase
DNA topoisomerase is incorrect. DNA topoisomerase is involved in forming the helical structure of DNA.

RNA polymerase
RNA polymerase is incorrect. RNA polymerase forms RNA strands to be used as a template for DNA transcription. Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia

Serine protease
Serine protease is incorrect. Serine proteases are a group of enzymes capable of cleaving protein bonds, responsible for degradation of proteins into smaller proteins or constituent amino acids.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with increasing shortness of breath and three episodes of syncope, a few months after the birth of her second child. On examination, her BP is 145/84 mmHg, her pulse is 80 bpm and regular. Her chest appears clear on auscultation. An echocardiogram is arranged, which shows elevated rightsided pressures, and pulmonary hypertension is confirmed on cardiac catheterisation. It is decided to start her on bosentan. Which one of the following correctly describes the mode of action of bosentan?
options: Endothelin A and B receptor antagonist
explanation:
Endothelin A and B receptor antagonist
Endothelin A receptors are thought to mediate vasoconstriction and smooth muscle cell proliferation in the pulmonary vasculature, whereas endothelin B receptors mediate production of nitric oxide and prostacyclin.

Angiotensin receptor blocker
Angiotensin receptor blocker is incorrect. Angiotensin receptor antagonists block the effects of angiotensin II, predominantly in the peripheral vasculature.

Endothelin A receptor antagonist
Endothelin A receptor antagonist is incorrect. Ambrisentan is a selective endothelin A receptor antagonist, which might allow more specific relaxation of pulmonary arterioles than bosentan.

Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor
Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor is incorrect. Phosphodiesterase type-5 inhibitors include sildenafil, which plays a supportive role in treating pulmonary hypertension.

Prostaglandin receptor inhibitor
Prostaglandin receptor inhibitor is incorrect. Prostaglandin infusions may be used to offer short-term reduction of pulmonary artery pressure.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with palpitations and shortness of breath. She has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), managed with high-dose Seretide, and an echocardiogram conducted 2 months earlier has revealed left atrial enlargement and mild mitral regurgitation. Examination reveals a BP of 115/75 mmHg, pulse is 145/min (atrial fibrillation). Serum creatinine is measured at 90 μmol/l. You elect to begin loading with digoxin. What is the pharmacokinetic basis for using a loading regimen for digoxin?
explanation:
Volume of distribution
The volume of distribution for digoxin is very large (510 l). This means that administered doses are rapidly distributed to body tissues and blood concentrations fall rapidly. Two to three initial loading doses are administered 6–8 h apart, which results in tissue saturation so that blood digoxin concentrations can then be maintained by regular maintenance doses. Commencing treatment without a loading regimen may typically take several days to reach therapeutic concentrations.

Gastrointestinal absorption
Gastrointestinal absorption is incorrect. Gastrointestinal absorption is high at approximately 60% after oral tablet administration.

Half-life
Half-life is incorrect. The elimination half-life is some 30–40 h in patients with normal renal function. Digoxin is renally excreted, and in patients with abnormal renal function the half-life may be as long as 100 h. This drives reduced dosing in patients with renal impairment.

Hepatic metabolism
Hepatic metabolism is incorrect. Hepatic metabolism has little significant effect on digoxin clearance, and no impact on the need for a loading regimen.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is seen as a follow-up in the Rheumatology Clinic. She is treated with NSAIDs and highdose methotrexate for severe rheumatoid arthritis. She has chronic kidney disease and a recent estimated glomerular filtration rate was 38 ml/min. She complains of increasing nausea and indigestion. She has recently been found to have high blood pressure and started on a new medication by her doctor. Which of the following medications should be used with the greatest caution?
explanation:
Omeprazole
Methotrexate is a substrate for organic anion transporter 1 (OAT-1) renal transporter and its levels are therefore affected by decreased renal function. OAT-1 inhibitors include drugs such as probenecid and therefore should not be used in conjunction with methotrexate. Omeprazole is also known to affect clearance of methotrexate; this interaction is not thought to be via OAT-1, but thought to be related to inhibition of breast cancer resistance protein, which is responsible for methotrexate transport within the kidney.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine has no significant impact on methotrexate clearance and does not require dose adjustment in renal failure.

Bisoprolol
Bisoprolol may accumulate in patients with severe renal impairment and may require dose reduction. This can be monitored relatively easily by clinical assessment, thereby posing less risk than omeprazole.

Gaviscon ®
Gaviscon ® is not expected to have any significant impact upon methotrexate metabolism. It may not be an ideal choice here, however, because it contains a significant amount of sodium.

Famotidine
Famotidine is comparatively safe in renal impairment (although the dose is halved, or the dosing interval doubled, in patients with a glomerular filtration rate of < 50). It has no effect on the clearance of methotrexate and is therefore a safer option in this patient than proton pump inhibitor therapy.

stem: A 62-year-old man who takes multiple medications for cardiovascular disease and diabetes comes to the clinic for review. He has been complaining of a blue discoloration to his vision over the past 5 weeks since his last medication review. Examination does not reveal any significant change in acuity over the past 6 months and no abnormality is seen on fundoscopy. Which of the following medications he is taking is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Sildenafil
Sildenafil is a PDE-5 inhibitor, but at high doses it also inhibits retinal PDE-6 isoenzymes, which leads to blue discoloration of vision. This can often be managed by reducing the dose of sildenafil. It is an expected adverse effect of all PDE-5 inhibitors when used at high dose.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is incorrect. Amlodipine may rarely cause diplopia.

Digoxin
Digoxin is incorrect. Digoxin is recognised at potentially toxic levels to lead to xanthopsia, or yellowing of vision, often in the context of digoxin toxicity rather than therapeutic drug concentrations.

Ramipril
Ramipril is incorrect. There are infrequent reports of conjunctivitis related to ramipril.

Sitagliptin
Sitagliptin is incorrect. Reports of hypoglycaemia and dizziness may occur after sitagliptin, but disturbance of colour vision has not been described.

stem: Which of the following is the most effective intervention?
explanation:
IV fomepizole
The clinical scenario is suggestive of toxic alcohol poisoning, eg by methanol, ethylene glycol, or glycol ethers. The metabolic acidosis with raised anion gap, and clinical features of intoxication, indicate moderate to severe toxicity, and haemodialysis may be considered. IV fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole) is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase and prevents metabolism of toxic alcohol to toxic anions that cause kidney disease and metabolic acidosis. IV ethanol can be used as an alternative, but may worsen intoxication, requires close monitoring and may cause pancreatitis.

Forced alkaline diuresis
Forced alkaline diuresis is incorrect. Forced alkaline diuresis was formerly used in the treatment of aspirin overdose but is rarely used now; it requires administration of large quantities of sodium bicarbonate to create alkaline urine and may cause profound hypokalaemia.

Gastric lavage
Gastric lavage is incorrect. Gastric lavage is rarely effective, if ever, and poses a number of technical hazards, with the result that it is now rarely used in clinical practice.

IV N-acetylcysteine
IV N-acetylcysteine is incorrect. Acetylcysteine is not expected to be helpful for toxic alcohol poisoning, but coadministration of acetylcysteine may be considered if there is a possibility that the patient could have ingested paracetamol.

IV sodium bicarbonate
IV sodium bicarbonate is incorrect. Sodium bicarbonate may be needed to control acid–base distrurbance and lessen the risk of kidney disease due to deposition of oxylate crystals, but would not address the underlying toxic cause.

stem: You are taking part in a study for a new anti-epileptic from the same chemical series as phenytoin, but thought to be associated with fewer adverse events. The company plans to institute therapeutic drug monitoring. What is the major reason for therapeutic drug monitoring for drugs like phenytoin?
explanation:
Narrow therapeutic range
Therapeutic drug monitoring is either pharmacokinetic (measuring drug concentration) or pharmacodynamic (measuring the effect of the drug clinically). Phenytoin is subject to therapeutic drug monitoring because concentrations higher than the therapeutic range indicate a high risk of neurological toxicity. The principles for therapeutic drug monitoring are: a relationship between plasma drug concentration and pharmacological effect knowledge of the drug level will influence management narrow therapeutic window possible patient compliance problems dose cannot be optimised by clinical observation alone.

CYP450 inhibition
CYP450 inhibition is incorrect. Measured drug concentrations would not help to determine the extent of any hepatic enzyme (CYP450) inhibition.

Hepatotoxicity at the therapeutic dose
Hepatotoxicity at the therapeutic dose is incorrect. If hepatotoxicity were predictably associated with high drug concentrations, then this would be a valid reason for therapeutic drug monitoring. If hepatotoxicity occurs at therapeutic drug concentrations, these would not be helpful.

Interaction protein bound agents co-prescribed
Interaction protein bound agents co-prescribed is incorrect. Co-administration of a drug with high protein binding might increase the free drug concentrations of certain drugs, but this by itself would be a less compelling indication for therapeutic drug monitoring.

Nephrotoxicity at the therapeutic dose
Nephrotoxicity at the therapeutic dose is incorrect. Therapeutic drug monitoring is not of particular value for predicting the occurrence of adverse effects, such as npehrotixicity, that occur within the normal therapeutic range of concentrations.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hyponatraemia?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
explanation:
Diuretic use
Thiazide diuretic use is a common cause of hyponatraemia, which is more likely to occur with advancing age due to impaired homeostatic mechanisms. In patients who present with chronic confusion, hyponatraemia should be considered, and the thiazide should be switched to an alternative anti-hypertensive.

Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is incorrect. The BMI is normal range with no reported weight gain, which makes chronic hypothyroidism less likely for the purposes of this question.

Polydipsia
Polydipsia is incorrect. There is no evidence that this patient has polydipsia.

Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is incorrect. SIADH is possible, although this diagnosis can only be made in the presence of euvolaemia and patients cannot be receiving diuretic therapy.

Urinary tract infection
Urinary tract infection is incorrect. Urinary infection alone would not be expected to cause hyponatraemia, unless complicated by dehydration or nephropathy.

stem: A 42-year-old patient who received a renal transplant some 4 months earlier comes to the Emergency Department complaining of nausea, anorexia and lethargy, which have increased over the past 2 weeks since a new medication was started for control of her blood pressure. She is taking a ciclosporin-based immunosuppressive regimen. On examination her BP is 123/82 mmHg; pulse is 80/min and regular. Her BMI is 22. There is an abdominal scar covering the recent transplant. Blood work reveals a 30% rise in creatinine over the past 2 weeks, and ciclosporin above the upper limit of the normal range. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Verapamil
It is important to be cautious with respect to introducing inhibitors of CYP 3A4 in conjunction with ciclosporin. Inhibitors of 3A4 where significant caution is advised include verapamil, diltiazem, imidazole anti-fungals and macrolide antibiotics.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is incorrect. Amlodipine is a substrate of 3A4, rather than being a potent inhibitor or inducer.

Bisprolol
Bisprolol is incorrect. Bisoprolol undergoes dual P450 metabolism via 2D6 and 3A4.

Ramipril
Ramipril is incorrect. Ramipril is metabolised to an active metabolite, ramiliprat, by the liver, but does not interfere with ciclosporin levels.

Valsartan
Valsartan is incorrect. Valsartan is metabolised predominantly by CYP 2C9, and there is no significant interaction with ciclosporin.

stem: A 65-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is prescribed a course of cefalexin for a respiratory tract infection. Which of the following correctly reflects the mode of action of cefalexin?
options: Binds to the 30s subunit of the ribosome
Binds to the 50s subunit of the ribosome
explanation:
Disrupts cell wall formation
Cephalosporins disrupt the synthesis of the peptidoglycan layer forming the bacterial cell wall, in a similar way to other β-lactams, including pencillins.

Binds to bacterial dihydrofolate reductase
Binds to bacterial dihydrofolate reductase is incorrect. Trimethoprim binds to bacterial dihydrofolate reductase, disrupting DNA synthesis.

Binds to the 30s subunit of the ribosome
Binds to the 30s subunit of the ribosome is incorrect. Tetracyclines bind to the 30s subunit of the bacterial ribosome.

Binds to the 50s subunit of the ribosome
Binds to the 50s subunit of the ribosome is incorrect. Macrolides inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 50s ribosomal subunit.

Leads to DNA fragmentation
Leads to DNA fragmentation is incorrect. Quinolones inhibit topoisomerase II and IV ligases, leading to DNA fragmentation and disruption of bacterial cell proliferation.

stem: You are drawing up guidelines for the use of insulin glargine in basal bolus regimes ahead of isophane insulin. When considering your guidelines, in which of the following situations does insulin glargine have the clearest advantage over isophane?
options: In patients with type-1 diabetes who have significant daytime hypoglycaemia on isophane
In patients with type-1 diabetes who have significant nocturnal hypoglycaemia on isophane
In patients with type-2 diabetes who are taking more than 15 U of isophane per day
In patients with type-2 diabetes who have episodes of daytime hypoglycaemia on isophane
In patients with type-2 diabetes who have weight gain on isophane
explanation:
In patients with type-1 diabetes who have significant nocturnal hypoglycaemia on isophane
The greatest benefit with respect to reduction in the absolute number of nocturnal hypoglycaemic events for glargine versus Humulin insulin is in Type 1 diabetes patients. HbA1c results are similar between treated groups.

In patients with type-1 diabetes who have significant daytime hypoglycaemia on isophane
In patients with type-1 diabetes who have significant daytime hypoglycaemia on isophane is incorrect. Day time hypoglycaemia is not significantly impacted by switching to glargine.

In patients with type-2 diabetes who are taking more than 15 U of isophane per day
In patients with type-2 diabetes who are taking more than 15 U of isophane per day is incorrect. The benefit of glargine over other types of insulin in reducing hypogly-caemia is in patients with type 1, rather than type 2 diabetes. NICE only recommends use of insulin glargine in patients with type-2 diabetes who have significant hypoglycaemia on iso-phane insulin.

In patients with type-2 diabetes who have episodes of daytime hypoglycaemia on isophane
In patients with type-2 diabetes who have episodes of daytime hypoglycaemia on isophane is incorrect. NICE recommends use of insulin glargine in patients with type-2 dia-betes who have significant hypoglycaemia on isophane insulin, but the greatest improvement would be for nocturnal hypoglycaemia. Diabetes - Type I

In patients with type-2 diabetes who have weight gain on isophane
In patients with type-2 diabetes who have weight gain on isophane is incorrect. NICE only recommends use of insulin glargine in patients with type-2 diabetes who have significant hypoglycaemia on isophane insulin.

stem: You are trialling a new antihypertensive agent, ‘Wonderone’. As part of the drug development programme, you must assess the half-life of Wonderone; some results are sent to you for calculation of the half-life: 15 min after subcutaneous injection: Wonderone level 150 U/l 2 h 15 min after subcutaneous injection: Wonderone level 37.5 U/l 4 h 15 min after subcutaneous injection: Wonderone level 9.4 U/l Which of the following stems fits best with the half-life of this agent?
explanation:
1 hr
The half-life is defined as the time taken for plasma levels of a particular chemical entity to fall by 50%. These results indicate that levels fall by 75% every 2 h (decline to 25% of the original level); hence, the half-life is calculated to be 1 hr. It is worth noting that a halving of plasma levels may not indicate a 50% reduction in activity of the agent, as a number of agents are metabolised to products that are also therapeutically or metabolically active.

90 min
90 min is incorrect. A 90-minute half-life would mean that it would take 3 hr for the plasma levels to reduce to 25% of the start point.

15 min
15 min is incorrect. Given the drug is delivered subcutaneously, it is likely that 15 minutes is the time taken to reach peak concentration in plasma, or T-max.

2 hr
2 hr is incorrect. If the half-life were 2 hours, it would take 4 hours for levels to reach 25% of the original measured value.

3 hr
3 hr is incorrect. If the half-life were 3 hours, it would take 6 hours for levels to reach 25% of the original measured value.

stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Arrange a fine needle aspiration (FNA) of the thyroid
Arrange an ultrasound of the thyroid
explanation:
Observe
This woman has evidence of very mild biochemical hyperthyroidism against a background of severe symptoms of hyperemesis gravidarum. Normal thyroid, on examination, and negative thyroid autoantibodies reduce the likelihood of a thyroid condition being the cause of her symptoms. Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) stimulates production of thyroid hormone in a similar way to thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), hence the biochemistry seen here, with a suppressed TSH, triiodothyronine (T3) just above the normal range and an elevated thyroxine (T4). Hyperemesis usually subsides by the 20th week of pregnancy, and intervention with antithyroid drugs is not indicated.

Start carbimazole
Start carbimazole is incorrect. The biochemical changes here are consistent with hyperemesis. Both propylthiouracil and carbimazole may be used in pregnancy, although there is little difference in the profile of the drugs in early pregnancy, propylthiouracil should not be used in the later stages, so many physicians use carbimazole throughout for patients with proven thyrotoxicosis.

Start propylthiouracil
Start propylthiouracil is incorrect. Propylthiouracil is an alternative therapy for bone fide thyrotoxicosis in pregnancy, but should be stopped in the third trimester; it should be avoided here as it is not indicated for hyperemesis.

Arrange a fine needle aspiration (FNA) of the thyroid
Arrange a fine needle aspiration (FNA) of the thyroid is incorrect. It is not indicated due to there being no underlying thyroid disease. Prescribing Safely (Breastfeeding and Pregnancy)

Arrange an ultrasound of the thyroid
Arrange an ultrasound of the thyroid is incorrect. Ultrasound should be avoided here, there being no indication of thyroid disease, and a scan may reveal an incidental finding that is innocuous and only builds anxiety.

stem: Insulin therapy was started. Which of the following is an action of insulin?
explanation:
Increased protein synthesis
Insulin is an anabolic hormone and acts to promote glucose uptake (and inhibit its generation or release), and its conversion into storage molecules (glycogen, or triglycerides). It acts to encourage growth in times of energy excess, hence promoting protein synthesis.

Conversion of glycogen to glucose
Conversion of glycogen to glucose is incorrect. In fact, insulin inhibits glycogenolysis and promotes glycogen synthesis, in order to store the relative excess of serum glucose after eating. It is an anabolic hormone and promotes protein synthesis.

Increased gluconeogenesis
Increased gluconeogenesis is incorrect. Insulin instead inhibits gluconeogenesis; insulin is released in response to an excess of serum glucose, usually after a meal. Therefore, the main actions of insulin are to promote the uptake and storage of this energy; there would be no sense in insulin increasing glucose levels through producing glucose from non-carbohydrate sources (i.e. gluconeogenesis). Insulin is an anabolic hormone and promotes protein synthesis.

Increased lipolysis
Increased lipolysis is incorrect. Insulin instead promotes lipid synthesis, stimulating cells to take up blood glucose and convert it to triglycerides. Insulin is an anabolic hormone and promotes protein synthesis.

Increases serum potassium levels
Increases serum potassium levels is incorrect. Insulin stimulates potassium uptake by cells, reducing serum potassium. This is because it affects the actions of the membrane NaKATPase. Insulin is an anabolic hormone and it will increase protein synthesis. A urine specimen is sent to you for analysis from a local general practitioner. The clinical information tells you that the urine is repeatedly tinged green or blue. It also tells you he has multiple underlying pathologies.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Haematology Clinic for review. He has suffered a second significant episode of haemolysis in the past year and is unable to complete his A-levels due to chronic illness. You plan to commence him on eculizumab therapy. Which of the following represents the mode of action of eculizumab?
explanation:
C5 inhibitor
Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, (PNH), is a clonal red cell abnormality which leaves erythrocytes open to complement mediated attack. This can occur in paroxysms resulting in significant haemolysis, Eculizumab is an orphan drug for PNH which inhibits C5, thus halting complement mediated erythrocyte destruction.

Anti-CD20
Anti-CD20 is incorrect. Rituximab is an example of an anti-CD20 MAb, which depletes B lymphocytes. It therefore has a role in antibody mediated autoimmune diseases.

Anti-TNF
Anti-TNF is incorrect. TNF antagonists such as infliximab are used primarily in the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis.

CTLA4 Ig
CTLA4 Ig is incorrect. CTLA4 Ig, abatacept, interferes with T cell co-stimulation and is used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis.

PD-1 inhibitor
PD-1 inhibitor is incorrect. PD-1 inhibitors increase T cell activity against cancer targets, they are not used in the treatment of autoimmune disease.

stem: You note an INR value which is significantly elevated at 7.5 on receipt at the lab. Apparently, the patient is taking 5 mg of warfarin per day and has been for some years. Which of the following co-medications is most likely to be the problem?
explanation:
Allopurinol
Allopurinol is recognised to increase INR by inhibiting the metabolism of warfarin. Out of the agents listed it is this therefore which is most likely to have led to the increase in INR.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is incorrect. Carbamazepine is known to induce a number of P450 enzymes including 1A2, 2B6, 2C9, 2C19 and 3A4, 5 and 7. As such it is more likely to decrease INR.

Modafinil
Modafinil is a hepatic inducer and therefore lead to reduced levels of warfarin.

Rifampicin
Rifampicin is incorrect. Rifampicin is an inducer of a wide range of CYP450 enzymes and thus leads to a decrease in INR in patients co-prescribed warfarin.

St John’s Wort
St John’s Wort is incorrect. St John’s Wort is increasingly popular as a herbal medication for depression, but induces a wide range of P450 enzymes, and hence results in a decrease in INR.

stem: His ECG shows tall, peaked T-waves. Which of the following management strategies is most effective at reducing serum potassium levels?
explanation:
10 units actrapid in 50 ml 50% dextrose
This therapy is the most effective way of reducing serum potassium levels. It will typically lower the potassium (K) by 1 mmol/l. It works by acting on Na-K ATPase channels to increase cellular uptake of K.

Calcium gluconate 10% 10 ml
Calcium gluconate 10% 10 ml is incorrect. This has no effect at lowering the potassium, but should be the first thing given to this patient as a cardioprotective drug in the setting of hyperkalaemia given the presence of peaked T-waves on the ECG.

Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg
Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg is incorrect. It acts on Na-K ATPase channels to cause potassium to shift into cells, but is not as effective as insulin-dextrose infusion. It typically lowers the potassium by 0.5–1 mmol/l, but the response can be variable and 20–40% of patients may only have a lowering of potassium of <0.5 mmol/l.

Sodium bicarbonate 1.26% 500 ml
Sodium bicarbonate 1.26% 500 ml is incorrect. There is no evidence to suggest this has benefit to lower potassium.

Calcium resonium 15 mg
Calcium resonium 15 mg is incorrect. It is a cation-exchange resin with a slow onset of action and is not indicated in the acute treatment of hyperkalaemia. Potassium Imbalance You are asked to review a 35-year-old woman who is undergoing chemotherapy for carcinoma of the breast, and has been admitted with febrile neutropenia. She is recognised to be severely allergic to penicillin so has been treated with a combination of vancomycin and aztreonam. Despite this she is continuing to spike fevers some 4 days after admission. Repeat neutrophil count is 0.5 × 10 9/l and CRP is still markedly elevated. Bacterial cultures have proved negative so far.

stem: What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Propylthiouracil
This patient has hyperthyroidism and her investigations confirm Graves’ disease as the cause. If she was not pregnant, carbimazole would be the first line treatment; however, this is teratogenic, especially in the first trimester. Despite propylthiouracil also being teratogenic, it is safer in the first trimester than carbimazole. As propylthiouracil does cross the placenta, the lowest dose possible should be used.

Carbimazole
Carbimazole is incorrect. This patient has symptoms and investigations consistent with Graves’ disease. Both carbimazole and propylthiouracil therapy are teratogenic. The risk of carbimazole therapy outweighs that of propylthiouracil in the first trimester; however, the risk of untreated Graves’ disease means treatment is indicated. Therefore, propylthiouracil is the appropriate therapy.

Levothyroxine
Levothyroxine is incorrect. Levothyroxine would be used to treat hypothyroidism, but this patient has hyperthyroidism; in fact her investigations are consistent with Graves’ disease. The most appropriate antithyroid treatment would be propylthiouracil.

Radioiodine
Radioiodine is incorrect. This patient has Graves’ disease, and although radioiodine therapy is an appropriate treatment option for this condition, this patient is pregnant. Pregnancy is an absolute contraindication for radioiodine therapy, and therefore this cannot be the correct answer.

Total thyroidectomy
Total thyroidectomy is incorrect. This patient has Graves’ disease, for which thyroidectomy is a potential treatment; however, she is pregnant. Undergoing surgery in pregnancy is best avoided where at all possible, due to the risk of fetal death, especially in an early pregnancy such as this. Surgery would only be advised for pressure symptoms secondary to a large goitre or after failed medical treatment. Propylthiouracil would be a much more appropriate treatment. Prescribing Safely (Breastfeeding and Pregnancy).

stem: A 42-year-old man comes in for review of his anti-hypertensive medication. He is currently managed on four agents and a statin, as he also has hypercholesterolaemia. He has suffered two episodes in the last 6 months where he has presented to the Emergency Department with features of facial angioedema. His BP in the clinic is 142/82 mmHg. Which of the following is most likely to be responsible for this symptom?
explanation:
Ramipril
Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are associated with angioneurotic oedema And is a common side effect. It can often be a delayed side effect.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is incorrect. Amlodipine, like other dihydropyridine calcium antagonists, tends to be associated with peripheral rather than facial oedema

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect. Uncommonly aspirin may trigger angioedema, especially in patients with C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency.

Bendroflumethiazide
Bendroflumethiazide is incorrect. Bendroflumethiazide is not a recognised cause of oedema.

Moxonidine
Moxonidine is incorrect. While Moxonidine is recognised to be associated with intermittent facial oedema, particularly affecting the eyelids ACE inhibitors are a more well recognised cause of angioedema.

stem: She is intubated and ventilated, and intravenous (IV) fluid replacement is commenced. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her lithium overdose?
explanation:
Haemodialysis
Recommendations for progression to haemodialysis in lithium overdose include: Serum lithium concentration is > 5 mmol/l Serum lithium concentration is > 4 mmol/l in patients with renal impairment (creatinine > 150 µmol/l) Decreased level of consciousness, seizure or life-threatening complications, irrespective of the serum lithium concentration Lithium concentration is > 2.5 mmol/l and the patient has signs of significant lithium toxicity (eg seizures, decreased consciousness), has renal insufficiency or other conditions that limit lithium excretion or suffers from an illness that would be worsened by aggressive IV fluid hydration, eg cardiac failure.

Activated charcoal via nasogastric (NG) tube
Charcoal does not bind lithium. It therefore has no role in the management of lithium overdose. It is given in paracetamol overdose and aspirin overdose.

Gastric lavage
Gastric lavage has no role in the management of lithium overdose. It was routinely recommended in patients presenting early after tricyclic antidepressant overdose, although this is no longer endorsed by many guidelines.

IV sodium bicarbonate
IV sodium bicarbonate is indicated for tricyclic antidepressant overdose where seizures occur and where there is significant QRS prolongation. In this situation, progression to haemodialysis is the only appropriate option. Lithium Toxicity A 50-year-old man from India was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and started on quadruple antituberculosis (TB) therapy two months ago. For the last three weeks, he has experienced progressive visual disturbance, particularly colour blindness. He was referred urgently to the Ophthalmology Clinic where clinical examination showed reduced visual acuity of both eyes with normal fundoscopy. On examination, his temperature is 36.7 °C, his pulse is 120 bpm, and his blood pressure is 130/60 mmHg. Investigations:

Whole bowel irrigation
Whole bowel decontamination with polyethylene glycol is an option for lesser degrees of lithium overdose. At this point, with very high lithium levels and significant signs of toxicity, haemodialysis is the only practical option.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She has recently been diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease and she is to be started on oral prednisolone. She is worried about side-effects of steroid therapy. Which of the following is well recognised as a main adverse effect of steroid therapy?
explanation:
Increased gluconeogenesis
Corticosteroids lead to insulin resistance, one consequence of which is increased gluconeogenesis. In some patients already at risk of diabetes mellitus, this can precipitate hyperglycaemia which requires treatment with oral medication, or insulin if hyperglycaemia is more significant. This increase in insulin resistance can also drive a need for treatment intensification in patients already diagnosed with diabetes.

Hypersomnia
